study.title: Matthew 19: marriage, discipleship and the reversal of the Kingdom
study.overview: In this chapter, Jesus continues on his way to Jerusalem and teaches on three central themes of discipleship: marriage and divorce, the welcome of children, and the cost of following Christ. He confronts convenient interpretations of the law, reaffirms God's purpose for marriage, corrects human values of greatness and wealth, and ends with a typical reversal of the Kingdom: many who seem first will end last, and vice versa. The chapter shows that entering eternal life does not depend on human merit, but on the grace of God, and that following Jesus requires absolute priority over possessions, status and security.

outline.title: Jesus teaches about marriage, divorce and celibacy
outline.explanation: Jesus answers the Pharisees' question about divorce, refers to the principle of creation and affirms the permanence of marriage. Then, in answering the disciples, it shows that not everyone receives the same vocation, and that there are people called to live without marrying because of the Kingdom.

outline.title: Children received by Jesus and the wealthy young man
outline.explanation: The disciples try to prevent the rapprochement of children, but Jesus welcomes them and declares that the Kingdom belongs to those who look like them. Then a young man asks about eternal life; Jesus calls him to an obedience that includes radical detachment, but the boy goes away sad because of his many possessions.

outline.title: Danger of wealth and the reward of discipleship
outline.explanation: Jesus teaches that wealth can make entry into the Kingdom extremely difficult and that salvation is impossible for human beings, but possible for God. He also promises reward those who have left everything because of his name and concludes with the reversal: the first will be last, and the last, first.

study.context: By the notes, Jesus is moving towards Jerusalem at a final stage of instruction of the disciples. This helps to understand the tone of the chapter: it is not about abstract teaching, but of preparation for the journey that will culminate in the cross. The Pharisees' debate on divorce also appears, in which there were divergent interpretations within Judaism regarding legitimate grounds for separation.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that God's purpose for marriage is stable union and not easy rupture; therefore, Jesus treats divorce as a concession linked to the hardness of the human heart, and not as a divine ideal. It also states that the Kingdom welcomes the humble and dependents, like children, while attachment to goods can prevent the obedient response to the call of Jesus. In the case of the rich young man, the problem is not simply to possess things, but to be possessed by them, because his wealth functions as God's rival. The teaching about salvation is clear: the human being cannot save himself for himself, and everything depends on the power of God. Finally, the reward promised to the disciples shows that the Kingdom redefines prestige, authority, and value; what is exalted now can be relegated, and what is despised now can be exalted by God.

scholarViews.insight: The Pharisees represented two divergent readings about divorce, one more restrictive and the other more permissive, and Jesus responds by affirming only one legitimate reason for separation: marital infidelity.
Jesus goes toward Jerusalem, and this stage of the way serves as an occasion to instruct the disciples before the final events of his earthly ministry.

questions: What does this chapter reveal about the difference between human concessions and God's original purpose for marriage?
In which areas of life can I be appearing obedient, but still retaining what occupies the place of God in my heart?
How can the Kingdom logic in which the latter can be first - confronts my criteria of success, status and security?
study.practice: Examine honestly what you call security: goods, reputation, relationships or control. Bring this before Christ in prayer, asking for a free heart to obey. If you are married, treat your commitment to seriousness and faithfulness, seeking to preserve unity with humility and repentance. If you are not married, receive your condition as a vocation before God, without envying the way of others. Approach Jesus with the simplicity of a child: without claiming merit, without negotiating with pride, and willing to follow him where he calls.
study.uncertainty: The notes do not allow to safely determine all the geographical details of the expression "beyond the Jordan"; one of the sources points out the possibility that the locomotion would be by the river bank, and not necessarily to the other side. There is also an interpretative limit in 19:30: the notes link the phrase to the reversal between Jews and Gentiles or between the powerful and the humble, but the text itself allows more than one legitimate application. In addition, when dealing with 19:12, the language about "castrates" should be understood in Portuguese as people without the ability to generate children or without marriage life, without imposing speculation beyond the text.
